articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Vessels in Cuba, Targets Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 5, 2026, targeting entities and vessels within Cuba, alongside actions against cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations. This action includes the publication of a Cuba-related Determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, specifically targeting the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

Among the newly designated entities are Empresa Comercializadora de Servicios Tecnicos y Tecnologicos (TECNOSIME) and Empresa Importadora y Exportadora de Productos de la Electronica y las Comunicaciones (CUBAELECTRONICA), both state-owned enterprises based in Havana, Cuba. Additionally, two Cuban-flagged vessels, the LPG Tanker EMILIA and the Chemical/Products Tanker GLORIA C, have been added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

The designations also include individuals and entities linked to cyber-related activities, such as Kok Wa Chui from Madagascar and Yujing He from Cambodia. This broad action underscores OFAC's continued efforts to pressure the Cuban regime and disrupt illicit financial networks globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations, Amends Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities and financial networks.

In addition to the Iran-focused measures, OFAC also issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment likely pertains to specific authorized transactions or relief efforts within Venezuela, reflecting the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy in the region.

The Iran-related OFAC Alert published concurrently with these designations focuses on the Iranian shadow fleet's reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion, highlighting the Treasury's vigilance against deceptive shipping practices.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of International Development Bank
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank.

This amended general license replaces and supersedes the previous General License FF. It provides a limited period for the orderly cessation of dealings with the designated entity and its majority-owned subsidiaries, with a wind-down deadline of December 1, 2026.

The issuance of such a wind-down license is a common practice following new designations, allowing non-sanctioned parties to extricate themselves from prohibited transactions without incurring penalties, provided they adhere to the specified terms and deadlines.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Individuals and Entities Supporting North Korean IT Worker Schemes and Rwandan Military in DRC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in North Korean IT worker fraud schemes and those supporting the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and a financial institution for their role in destabilizing the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

Under the North Korea sanctions program, OFAC added several individuals, including Russian nationals Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov and Vitold Viktorovich Obertas, and North Korean national Han Yu Song, for their involvement with entities like LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER, which facilitate North Korean IT worker schemes. These schemes are known to generate revenue for North Korea's weapons programs.

For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, OFAC sanctioned the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Rwanda and Zigama Credit and Savings Society (Zigama CSS), a Kigali-based financial institution. These designations aim to hold Rwanda accountable for its alleged support of the M23 movement in eastern DRC.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services from the United States to JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was majority-owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, a designated Russian state-owned company, rendering MMZA a blocked person by operation of law, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until June 2022.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement emphasizes the importance of thorough sanctions-related diligence during acquisitions, continuous vigilance against sanctions risks, and robust oversight of foreign operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting Requirements
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended 11 of its Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, as part of an ongoing review to ensure its published guidance remains current.

The revised FAQs cover critical topics such as distinguishing between blocking and rejecting transactions, the interest required on blocked funds, permissible service charges on blocked accounts, and the timing and procedures for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions to OFAC.

These updates aim to provide clearer guidance for financial institutions and other U.S. persons on their compliance obligations, particularly regarding the proper handling and reporting of sanctions-related transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026, alongside the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses.

In a significant development, OFAC also removed certain individuals and entities from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under the Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs. Specifically, Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities (Shanghai Moxing Cultural Media Co. Ltd. and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio) were delisted from the North Korea program, and Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov was delisted from the Belarus program.
The new general licenses and amended FAQs reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting measures based on evolving foreign policy objectives and ongoing reviews of existing designations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Chinese Entities Under PAIPA, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026, targeting Chinese entities and adding them to its Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List (NS-MBS List).

Among the newly designated entities are BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND I), BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE II VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND II), and BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN ZHIYUAN ENTERPRISE MANAGEMENT CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP. These entities face various restrictions, including the blocking of property and prohibitions on loans from U.S. financial institutions exceeding $10,000,000 in any 12-month period.

Concurrently, OFAC issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Venezuela-related General License 60A on October 16, 2026, titled "Authorizing Transactions Related to Earthquake Relief Efforts in Venezuela."

This amended general license replaces and supersedes General License 60, extending the authorization period for earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela. Additionally, OFAC issued one amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to reflect the extended authorization end date.

The issuance of this general license underscores OFAC's commitment to facilitating humanitarian aid and disaster relief, even within sanctioned jurisdictions, by providing clear authorizations for necessary transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Individuals and Entities, Adds Cuban Entity to Sanctions List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 15, 2026, targeting 16 individuals and 10 entities for allegedly enabling sanctions evasion and sustaining Iran's military and proxy forces.

Among the designated parties are Iran-based banks Jazireh International Bank Company and Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company, which OFAC stated operated offshore in free trade zones, as well as Iran-based exchange houses and individuals involved in foreign exchange operations. Individuals such as Azadeh Abdolalipur, Milad Katebi, and Sadegh Bavi were also added to the SDN list.

Concurrently, OFAC announced a Cuba designation, adding Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) to its sanctions list pursuant to Executive Order 14404. This action further expands U.S. pressure on the Cuban financial sector.

articles.headline: Commerce Department Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced last week that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with the controls already applied to firearms, reducing the compliance burden on the firearms industry while maintaining national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and a BIS license will be required for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also apply to suppressors.

body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.
